transcript:
What a casting announcement to wake up to, cause we just found out that Reeve Carney and Evan Lobo Zada will be leading cabaret on the West End. And I am very excited, in part because Eva Noblezada is my favorite Sally I have ever seen. I thought that her Sally was revelatory, and so the fact that she is coming back is enough to get me excited. But then the fact that she's doing it alongside Reeve, I am so intrigued, because I think that he is going to be so different from every other MC that we've had. Like, this is going to be a rock star MC like we haven't seen before. I guess the closest would be Adam Lambert's MC, which is famously my favorite MC that I saw on Broadway. But Adam's vibe is also very different from Reeves, so, yeah, I'm very interested to see how he does in this role, especially because the MC is such an animated character, and Reeve's characters traditionally are not. So I feel like we're about to see a very different side from Reeve, performance wise, than we've ever seen before, and that's also really exciting. But, yeah, I think it's so cute that they're doing another show together. I think that Eve is gonna slay, and Reeve is a bit of a wild card, but I'm very excited to see what he does with it.

[Second video: I was excited to see this duo too, but now… 😳 #Broadway #CabaretMusic...]
We have to talk about this comment from Billy Porter with what's going on in the world right now. Yeah, um, you know, black people have replaced the Jews in this sort of configuration of what we're going through. So now I'm going to try and be charitable here in my interpretation of what he's saying, because I think what he is trying to say is that in today's day and age, black people face a lot of discrimination. And you can draw a lot of parallels to the discrimination that black people face and the discrimination that Jewish people face, which I think is a true statement. Where I take issue with this is this notion of black people replacing Jewish people, implying that Jews no longer face discrimination, which is just patently untrue. As we all know, anti Semitism is alive and well. And to me, it feels like Billy's comments here is dismissing that, which becomes even more problematic when you consider that he is about to step into a musical that is first and foremost about Jewish trauma. I certainly think that its themes around conformity and complacency are relevant beyond the Jewish community. And I really appreciate casting that is able to draw these parallels and show how the black community, for example, is also hurt by these very same factors. But it doesn't seem like Billy has an appreciation for that intersectionality. He only really seems interested at exploring black trauma at the expense Of Jewish trauma, which he seems to think, or at the very least imply, doesn't really exist anymore. Which is just fundamentally at odds with the piece that he is about to be performing eight times a week.
